—❗️🇮🇷/🇬🇧 BREAKING: Iranian hackers shut down a power plant in the UK for 4 consecutive days with a sophisticated cyber attack, according to [The Telegraph](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2026/08/22/iranian-hackers-shut-down-uk-power-plant/)
It is thought to be the first time that hackers affiliated with the Iranian government have succeeded in closing down such a facility in the UK, and believed to be the most successful cyber attack of its kind.
The incident took place at the same time as a series of attacks on U.S. water infrastructure last month, which affected 12 states and caused concern in the White House.

events.text:
💀 Musk’s FAA fix flops, opening the door for Palantir
The attempt to reform the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) with the involvement of Elon Musk’s DOGE has done little to solve the real problems facing the US air traffic control system. Instead of the promised rapid technological overhaul, hundreds of employees were shown the door, while Palantir took on an increasingly prominent role in its digital infrastructure.
DOGE cuts staff but crisis remains
DOGE became involved in the FAA overhaul in early 2025 amid growing concerns about outdated equipment, system failures and a chronic shortage of air traffic controllers. The goal was to streamline the agency and speed up modernization. Instead, around 400 FAA employees were reportedly dismissed, including staff responsible for maintaining and supporting critical infrastructure.
The FAA’s biggest problem remains a chronic shortage of air traffic controllers and technical personnel. Cutting hundreds of employees, including staff responsible for maintaining critical equipment, was unlikely to make the system more resilient. Continued outages and infrastructure failures highlight a fundamental issue – technology cannot simply replace experienced and highly qualified specialists.
Billions are now up for grabs
Yet the proposed answer to the crisis focuses on digital technologies and artificial intelligence. Congress has allocated $12.5 billion to modernize the US air traffic control system, with roughly $5 billion set aside for software and technology upgrades. For companies already operating within the FAA’s digital ecosystem, this represents a potentially enormous opportunity. [Palantir’s Foundry platform](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70382) is already in use at the agency, putting the company in a strong position as new contracts are awarded.
Palantir already inside
Palantir had already established a presence within the FAA’s internal infrastructure while competing for a major AI contract to help [reshape air traffic control](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70034). Its existing role could give the company a valuable advantage as Washington prepares to spend billions of dollars on “modernizing” the nation’s aviation system.
The result is a striking irony: the US cuts the people keeping its skies safe, then turns to AI to fill the gap. The FAA’s problems remain unresolved. The staffing crisis persists, and the technology still has to prove it can do the job, but Palantir is already inside the system, waiting for its share.
